title: Conservation of energy — energy is never lost, only spread out
examTip: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated. If asked where wasted energy goes, say 'dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings'.
introTips: Think about a bouncing ball. Where does all its energy go?
Energy stores are like bank accounts. The total balance never changes.
The words 'lost' and 'used up' are banned in physics. Say 'dissipated' or 'transferred'.
intro: Drop a ball, turn on a light, or burn fuel in a car engine. Each time, energy changes form. It never disappears. It just moves. The law of conservation of energy explains two things. It is why your phone battery runs flat. It is why insulating your house saves money. All energy physics starts here. Know where energy really goes, not just where we want it to go.

keyPoints.heading: The law of conservation of energy
keyPoints.content: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred from one store to another. The total energy in a closed system always stays the same. This is one of the most basic laws in all of physics. Sometimes energy seems to have 'disappeared'. In fact, it has been transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings. We say it has been dissipated. A bouncing ball is a perfect example. As it bounces, gravitational potential energy changes to kinetic energy. On every impact, some energy heats the ball and floor. Some is transferred by sound waves. It all ends up in the thermal store of the surroundings. That is why each bounce is a little lower. The total mechanical energy falls with each bounce. But the total energy, including the energy dissipated, stays exactly the same.
writeBullets: Conservation of energy — energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred between stores
Closed system — a system where no energy enters or leaves from outside
Energy store — a way of holding energy (kinetic, gravitational potential, thermal, chemical and so on)
Dissipated — energy spread out into the surroundings, usually as thermal energy
Thermal store — the internal energy held by the particles of a substance

keyTerms.def: Energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred between stores
A system where no energy enters or leaves; total energy stays constant
Energy spread out into the surroundings, usually as thermal energy, where it is difficult to use again

keyPoints.memTip: Think of energy like money. You can move it between accounts. But you can never make it from nothing or make it vanish.
keyPoints.tutor_note: People often say energy is 'used up'. It isn't. Energy is transferred, never destroyed.

keyPoints.heading: Useful and wasted energy
keyPoints.content: In any energy transfer, some energy is usefully transferred. It does what we want. The rest is wasted, usually as heat or sound. A light bulb transfers electrical energy into two outputs. These are useful light energy and wasted thermal energy. The wasted thermal energy is the heat you feel near the bulb. A car engine changes chemical energy stored in fuel into useful kinetic energy. But it also wastes a lot as thermal energy in the engine and exhaust. Some is wasted as sound. Wasted energy is not 'lost'. It is just in a less useful form, spread into the surroundings. We can reduce wasted energy in several ways: - thermal insulation reduces the rate of cooling - lubrication reduces friction between moving parts, so less mechanical energy turns into heat - streamlining reduces air resistance, so less kinetic energy is wasted pushing through the air
writeBullets: Useful energy transfer — energy that goes to the output store we want
Wasted energy — energy transferred to a store we don't want, usually thermal or sound
Lubrication — using oil or grease between surfaces to reduce friction and heat wasted
Insulation — material that slows the rate of thermal energy transfer to the surroundings
Streamlining — shaping an object to reduce air resistance and cut wasted kinetic energy

keyTerms.def: Energy transferred to the intended output store
Energy transferred to an unintended store, usually thermal or sound
Using oil or similar material between surfaces to reduce friction and heat loss

keyPoints.memTip: Useful = what you WANT. Wasted = what you DON'T want.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Sankey diagrams are a great way to picture this. The width of each arrow shows the amount of energy.

keyPoints.heading: Energy dissipation
keyPoints.content: Dissipation means energy spreading out into the surroundings, almost always as thermal energy. Once energy has dissipated, it is very hard to use again. It is spread thinly across billions of particles and can't easily be collected back. Even tiny amounts of friction or air resistance slowly dissipate a moving object's energy. You can never get it back. Key examples of dissipation: - friction between surfaces: mechanical energy → thermal energy. Brakes get hot, and hands get warm when rubbed - electrical resistance in wires: electrical energy → thermal energy. This is how a kettle heats water. It is also why transmission cables waste energy - sound absorption by walls: energy transferred by sound waves is dissipated. It is stored in less useful ways in the thermal store of the walls
writeBullets: Dissipation — energy spreading out into the surroundings as thermal energy. This makes it hard to reuse
Friction — a force between surfaces that changes kinetic or mechanical energy into thermal energy
Electrical resistance — opposes the flow of current. A current in a wire heats the wire
Sound absorption — energy carried by sound waves is dissipated, so it is stored in less useful ways

keyTerms.def: The spreading of energy into the surroundings as thermal energy, making it hard to use again
A contact force between surfaces that converts kinetic energy to thermal energy

keyPoints.memTip: Dissipate = spread out and thin out. Like a drop of dye in a swimming pool, you can't collect it back.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Dissipated energy still obeys conservation. It still exists, but it is stored in less useful ways.

keyPoints.heading: Reducing unwanted energy transfers
keyPoints.content: Engineers and designers work hard to cut wasted energy in devices and buildings. Lubrication: oil between moving parts reduces friction. So less mechanical energy turns into unwanted thermal energy. It is used in car engines, bicycle chains and factory machines. Thermal conductivity: the higher the thermal conductivity, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across the material. Thermal insulation: materials with a low thermal conductivity slow down energy transfer. Energy moves more slowly from warm objects to cold surroundings. Examples: - fibre glass loft insulation traps air, which reduces conduction and convection - double glazing has an air gap between the panes, which reduces heat conduction - cavity wall insulation puts foam or fibre in the gap inside brick walls Walls of a building: thicker walls make a building cool more slowly. Walls with a lower thermal conductivity also make it cool more slowly. Testing insulators: you can compare materials as thermal insulators. Wrap the same amount of hot water in each material. Measure how much the temperature falls in a set time. The independent variable is the material. The dependent variable is the fall in temperature. Control variables include the volume of water, its starting temperature, the time and the thickness of material. Streamlining: giving vehicles and objects an aerodynamic shape reduces air resistance. So less kinetic energy is wasted pushing against drag. It is used in sports cars, aircraft and cyclists' helmets.
writeBullets: Lubrication — oil between moving parts reduces friction and cuts wasted thermal energy
Thermal conductivity — the higher it is, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction
Loft insulation — fibre glass traps air. This reduces heat loss through the roof by conduction and convection
Double glazing — air gap between panes reduces heat conduction through windows
Cavity wall insulation — foam or fibre in wall cavities slows heat transfer to the outside
Building walls — thicker walls with a lower thermal conductivity make a building cool more slowly
Testing insulators — change the material, measure the fall in temperature, keep everything else the same
Streamlining — an aerodynamic shape reduces drag. Less kinetic energy is wasted on air resistance

keyTerms.def: A material or design that slows the transfer of thermal energy to the surroundings
The higher the thermal conductivity, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction
Shaping an object to reduce air resistance and the kinetic energy lost to drag

keyPoints.memTip: LIS: Lubrication, Insulation, Streamlining. These are three ways to cut wasted energy.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Good thermal insulators have a low thermal conductivity. So energy is transferred through them slowly.

tables.title: Energy transfer examples — useful output, wasted output, and how waste is reduced

0.question: A ball is dropped and bounces several times before it stops. Which statement best explains where the energy goes?
options: It is transferred to the thermal store of the ball, floor and surroundings. It is dissipated as heat and sound
The energy is destroyed when the ball stops moving
The energy is stored in the gravitational potential store of the Earth
The energy disappears because no more work is being done
0.correctFeedback: Exactly right. The total energy is conserved. It is transferred to thermal stores (and some to sound), not destroyed.
0.wrongFeedback: Remember: energy is NEVER destroyed. When the ball stops, all its mechanical energy has been dissipated into the surroundings. It goes as thermal energy and sound.

1.question: An electric kettle heats some water. Which energy transfer is wasted?
options: Energy transferred to the thermal store of the kettle and the air around it
Energy transferred to the thermal store of the water
Energy transferred electrically to the kettle
Energy that is destroyed as the water boils
1.correctFeedback: Correct. The useful transfer is to the water. Energy that heats the kettle and the air is wasted.
1.wrongFeedback: The kettle's job is to heat the water, so that transfer is useful. Energy that heats the kettle and the air is wasted. Energy is never destroyed.

2.question: Which of the following is the best description of 'dissipation'?
options: Energy spreading out into the surroundings as thermal energy. This makes it hard to use again
Energy being destroyed when a machine stops working
Energy being stored in a chemical store for later use
Energy transferred usefully to the output device
2.correctFeedback: Spot on! Dissipated energy spreads out, so it is stored in less useful ways. It still exists, but it is very hard to collect back.
2.wrongFeedback: Dissipation doesn't mean energy is destroyed. It means energy spreads out as thermal energy into the surroundings. There it is very hard to collect and reuse.

3.question: A house has thick walls made of a material with a low thermal conductivity. What effect does this have?
options: Energy is conducted through the walls faster
Energy in the house is destroyed more slowly
3.correctFeedback: Correct. Thick walls with a low thermal conductivity reduce the rate of energy transfer. So the house cools more slowly.
3.wrongFeedback: A low thermal conductivity means a low rate of energy transfer by conduction. Thicker walls slow it down too. So the house cools more slowly.

commonMistakes: Saying energy is 'used up' or 'lost'. Energy is never destroyed. Say 'dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings'.
Mixing up energy 'stores' and energy 'transfers'. Stores are where energy sits (kinetic, gravitational PE, thermal). Transfers are how it moves (heating, working, radiation).
Thinking wasted energy breaks the conservation law. It doesn't. Wasted energy is still energy. It just ends up in a store we didn't want.
Saying thermal insulation 'stops heat'. It slows the rate of transfer. It doesn't stop it completely.
examTips: In any question about energy 'disappearing', say where it went. It has been dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings.
When asked how to reduce wasted energy, give a specific method. For example: lubrication, thermal insulation or streamlining. Then explain how it works.
Sankey diagrams are drawn to scale. The width of each arrow shows the amount of energy. All the arrows must add up to the input.
A 'closed system' means no energy enters or leaves. The total energy is always constant.
revisionCardBullets: Conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred between stores
In a closed system: total energy always stays the same
Useful energy: energy transferred to the output store we want
Wasted energy: energy transferred to a store we don't want, usually thermal or sound
Dissipation: energy spreading out as thermal energy into the surroundings. It is hard to reuse
Friction changes kinetic or mechanical energy → thermal energy (heat)
Electrical resistance changes electrical energy → thermal energy
Lubrication reduces friction → less thermal energy wasted
Thermal insulation (loft, double glazing, cavity walls) slows heat loss to the surroundings
Higher thermal conductivity → higher rate of energy transfer by conduction
Thicker walls with a lower thermal conductivity → a building cools more slowly
Streamlining reduces air resistance → less kinetic energy wasted
